title: Product of the Last K Numbers
description: Brute force to optimized: multiplying the last k numbers directly on every query versus a running prefix product answered with one division, reset on zero.

sections.title: Product of the Last K Numbers

content.title: Product of the Last K Numbers

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Design a class that supports add(num), appending an integer to a running stream, and getProduct(k), returning the product of the last k numbers in the stream. It is guaranteed getProduct will never be called with k larger than the stream's current length.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","A sequence of add(num) and getProduct(k) calls"],["Output","The result of every getProduct call"],["Goal","Answer getProduct quickly, without multiplying k numbers every single call"],["Constraints","0 <= num <= 100; 1 <= k <= 40000 calls total"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["A running PRODUCT over a growing stream needs fast range queries","Maintain a running prefix product, exactly like a prefix SUM, but with division for range queries"],["A zero anywhere in the last k numbers makes the product exactly 0","Reset the prefix product tracking whenever a zero is added, since division cannot \"skip over\" a zero"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Maintain a growing stream of numbers, supporting fast queries for the product of the most recent k numbers added.

blocks.title: Analogy: Tracking a Running Financial Growth Multiplier
blocks.text: Picture tracking a running multiplier representing cumulative growth over time (like compound interest factors), and needing to quickly answer "what was the combined growth over just the last k periods," without recomputing that combined growth from scratch each time.

blocks.caption: A zero anywhere in the window forces a product of 0; resetting avoids ever dividing by zero

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: add(3), add(0), add(2), add(5), add(4)
getProduct(2) is 5 times 4 = 20; getProduct(3) is 2 times 5 times 4 = 40; getProduct(4) spans the 0, giving 0.
5. How Should We Think?

Before multiplying the last k numbers directly on every call, notice a running prefix PRODUCT (analogous to a prefix sum) lets any range product be computed with one division, as long as no zero is involved.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A prefix sum lets any range sum be computed as one subtraction; a prefix PRODUCT similarly lets any range product be computed as one division, as long as no zero appears in that range.

Observation 2: A zero added to the stream makes the product of any window spanning it exactly 0, and dividing by zero (or by a prefix product that is zero) is undefined, so the running prefix product breaks at that point.

Observation 3: Resetting the prefix product list to start fresh right after a zero is added correctly handles this, since no later window can "see past" that zero anyway if its length keeps it within the reset segment; if a query's k exceeds the numbers added since the last zero, the answer must be 0.

Observation 4: This makes every add() an O(1) append, and every getProduct(k) an O(1) division (or an immediate 0 if k reaches past the last reset).

This leads to maintaining a running prefix product list, resetting it whenever a zero is added, and answering getProduct(k) with one division (or 0 if k exceeds what has accumulated since the last reset).
6. Brute Force Solution
Store every number added in a plain list, and on getProduct(k), multiply the last k numbers directly.
Step by step algorithm

items: add(num): append num to a list.
getProduct(k): multiply together the last k numbers in that list directly.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every getProduct call re-multiplies exactly the requested range from scratch.
With up to 40000 calls, and k potentially large each time, this repeats a lot of multiplication work.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) per add, O(k) per getProduct.
Space: O(n) for the stored numbers.
Limitation: if getProduct is called frequently with large k, repeatedly multiplying from scratch becomes the bottleneck; a running prefix product would make each query O(1).
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why multiplying from scratch each time is unnecessary: a running prefix product lets any suffix product be computed as a single division, exactly like a prefix sum enables O(1) range sums.

What breaks a running prefix product: a zero in the stream, since a prefix product hitting zero cannot be "divided back out" to recover values before it.

How to handle a zero cleanly: reset the prefix product list to just [1] right after a zero is added, effectively starting a fresh segment; any getProduct(k) reaching back past this reset point must return 0, since a zero is definitely within that range.

The core idea: maintain a prefix product list, resetting on zero, and answer getProduct(k) as the last prefix divided by the prefix from k steps back (or 0 if k reaches past the last reset).

Maintain a list of prefix products, starting with 1. On add(num), if num is 0, reset the list back to [1]; otherwise, append the last prefix times num. On getProduct(k), if k is at least the list's length, return 0 (a zero was reset within that range); otherwise, return the last prefix product divided by the prefix product k positions before it.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for add(3), add(0), add(2), add(5), add(4)

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: running prefix product, reset on zero, division for O(1) queries

blocks.text: Why This Works

As long as no zero lies within the queried window, dividing the latest prefix product by the prefix product from k steps back exactly cancels out everything before the window, leaving just the product of the last k numbers, in O(1). Resetting on a zero guarantees that if a query's k reaches back past that reset point, it necessarily spans the zero, and the answer is correctly 0 without any division needed.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) per add and per getProduct.
Space: O(n) for the prefix product list.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Product of the Last K Numbers is prefix sums adapted to products: division replaces subtraction for range queries, with the one added wrinkle that a zero anywhere breaks the technique and requires an explicit reset.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to reset the prefix product list on a zero, which would otherwise attempt to divide by zero or produce an incorrect result.
Not returning 0 immediately when k reaches past the last reset point, instead of trying (and failing) to compute a division-based answer.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["getProduct(k) where k spans a zero","Returns 0 directly, via the reset-detection check."],["No zero ever added","The prefix product list simply keeps growing, and every getProduct is a direct division."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly calling out the "prefix sum, but with products and a zero-triggered reset" framing shows the connection to a well-known technique clearly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "what breaks a running prefix product", think: a zero, since it can never be divided back out; reset the tracking there instead.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you support negative numbers in the stream as well?
How would you adapt this same idea to answer range MIN or MAX queries instead of products?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Prefix sums, the direct parent pattern, adapted here from addition/subtraction to multiplication/division.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs add in O(1) and getProduct in O(k). The optimized prefix-product approach runs both in O(1). Both use O(n) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a running prefix product, the multiplicative analog of prefix sums, with a reset on zero.
Core Idea: maintain a prefix product list, resetting to [1] on any zero; getProduct(k) is the last prefix divided by the prefix k steps back, or 0 if that reaches past the last reset.
Time: O(k) per getProduct for the brute force, O(1) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: a zero breaks the division-based prefix-product technique, requiring an explicit reset rather than special-case division logic.
Interview Difficulty: a clean extension of prefix sums, with the zero-handling being the one real subtlety.
One line memory trick: prefix products, division for queries, reset on zero.
